conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? My kidneys have been off for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s consistent with your stage 4 CKD. We’re avoiding nephrotoxic drugs. That’s why we chose cefazolin—it’s safer for your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve got enough problems without my kidneys crashing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also giving you heparin shots to prevent clots, since you’re not moving much. And we’d like you to sit up in the chair tomorrow if you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But I’ve got pain in my back and shoulders from sitting so long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can adjust your pain meds. You’re on oxycodone as needed. Let the nurse know if it’s not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back. It’s Morganella morganii, which is sensitive to several antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin and gentamicin. But again, without changing the nephrostomy, the infection may persist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I know. But I don’t want the tube changed here. Can’t I just take the pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can switch you to oral cefadroxil, which covers this bug. But please follow up with urology soon. This isn’t something to ignore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call them when I get home. Just get me through this recovery first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fair enough. Your flap is looking good—warm, pink, no signs of infection. You can start advancing your diet today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m tired of broth. Any word on when I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well, possibly tomorrow or the next day. We need to see your drain output go down and make sure you’re comfortable on oral pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your drain output is decreasing—only 25 mL yesterday. That’s a good sign. We’ll likely remove it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’ll be a relief. Can I shower with it still in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but keep the site clean and dry. Let the water run over it, then pat dry. Don’t submerge it. And keep the drain secured so it doesn’t pull.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I need to write down how much drains out each day, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Bring that log to your follow-up. Also, keep using the air mattress. No sitting or lying on your back for at least three weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember. Last time I didn’t, and it opened up. I’m not doing that again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Watch for redness, swelling, or darkening of the flap. If it turns blue or black, call your surgeon immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my seizures? I haven’t had one in months, but I’m on levetiracetam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on your regular dose. We haven’t changed any of your home meds except for pain and antibiotics. Keep taking them as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my depression meds? Escitalopram and trazodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re getting those too. We know mental health is part of recovery. If you’re feeling down or anxious, let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay. Just ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, you’re cleared for discharge. Your vital signs are stable, you’re eating well, and the drain output is low. We’ll remove the drain before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Finally. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the air mattress, keep the area clean and dry, monitor the incision, and record any drainage. Take cefadroxil twice a day for ten days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my nephrostomy? I’ll call urology, I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. You had a positive urine culture and fevers. This infection won’t go away on its own. Follow up within a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll see plastic surgery next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in seven to ten days. Call sooner if you have fever, increased pain, or flap changes. You’re going home with services—nursing will check on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll take care of this one. I don’t want to be back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re rooting for you. Take it slow, follow the instructions, and keep in touch. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. Tell the team thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a safe trip home. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—what about that lung nodule? Should I get it checked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as before, a follow-up CT in three months. Your primary team will coordinate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep taking your sevelamer with meals for your phosphate levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t missed a dose. My nephrologist would kill me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart. Alright, I’ll sign your discharge orders. The nurse will go over everything one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, doc. I mean it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly to remove the drain and finalize discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep up with your bowel regimen. We started you on something to help prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had issues before. I’ll keep using it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s all for now. Rest well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're in the hospital because of fever and flank pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this pus draining from my nephrostomy tube for weeks. Last few days it got worse—fever, chills, and the area’s swollen and tender.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve also had abdominal pain and back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and bladder spasms too. But my ileal conduit is draining fine—no issues there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Your labs show a high white blood cell count, which means your body is fighting an infection. We also did a CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there an abscess? I’ve had those before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No abscess on the scan. The nephrostomy tube is in the right place, and there’s no sign of a blockage. But the swelling and pus suggest cellulitis around the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s infected, but not in the kidney itself?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, it looks like a skin and soft tissue infection around the tube. We’ll treat it with IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Which one? I’ve got a lot of allergies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started meropenem because of your allergies. It covers a broad range of bacteria. But you had a rash after the first dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt itchy. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you Benadryl, and the rash improved. We’ll keep monitoring. The meropenem is still the best option for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the yeast in my urine? I saw that on the report.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw yeast and some strep in one sample, but later tests showed no growth. It may have been contamination. We’re not treating it unless it comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I’ve been nauseous too. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but nausea can also be a side effect of meropenem. We’ll watch it and give Zofran if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white count is coming down, which is a good sign. The swelling around the tube is less today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a bit better. Still nauseous, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep offering Zofran. Your blood cultures were negative, so no bloodstream infection. The bacteria from the tube site was staph, but sensitive to the antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the staph came from the skin around the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s a common skin bug. The meropenem is working well against it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray because you had a cough. It shows no pneumonia—just some atelectasis, which is common when you’re not moving much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing serious in my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, lungs look clear. Your kidney function is stable, and hemoglobin is around 8, which is your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about my kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest urine culture from both the nephrostomy tube and ileal conduit shows no growth. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the infection is gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The acute infection is resolving. We’ll finish the 7-day course of meropenem and switch to oral fosfomycin to prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fosfomycin? I’ve never taken that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a long-acting antibiotic, taken once a week. It’ll help protect your urinary system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No fever in over 48 hours. The induration around the tube is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you in a day or two. First, we need to confirm you’re stable off IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my nephrostomy tube? It still leaks sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you need a tube exchange. It’s scheduled in a few weeks, but we can move it up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed your meropenem course. We’ll start the first dose of fosfomycin today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How do I take it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dissolve the packet in water and drink it. You’ll take it weekly to prevent future infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—can I go back to them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home meds are being restarted—pain meds, seizure meds, omeprazole, and your kidney meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no nausea today. That’s great. We’ll discontinue the Zofran.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I think it was the meropenem. I feel better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll make a note for next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious. Can I have my clonazepam back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted your clonazepam. We checked your prescription history to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: labs are stable, no fever, and you’re eating well. We’re clearing you for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take fosfomycin weekly as prescribed. Keep the nephrostomy site clean and dry. Watch for redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled. Call interventional radiology to confirm the date. Also, follow up with your primary doctor and urologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I get my allergies checked? I don’t want to keep reacting to antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent idea. We recommend an outpatient allergy evaluation to clarify which antibiotics you can safely take.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain and anxiety meds—are they okay long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re appropriate for now, but your doctors may review the plan to ensure safety with long-term use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge orders are in. You’ll go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge summary. Take the first fosfomycin dose as directed. Call us if you develop fever or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call IR to confirm the tube swap.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. ___. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your mother is listed as your healthcare contact. We’ll make sure she has the instructions too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’ll help me at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll go over the wound care and medication list with her before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. I want to make sure I don’t miss anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you written instructions and schedule follow-ups. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again. I’m glad this infection is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. Take it easy, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly with your discharge meds and paperwork.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Just keep up with the care plan, and you should stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you with transfer to the wheelchair shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re feeling better. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in because your left nephrostomy tube stopped draining and you’ve had severe flank pain. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I woke up and noticed no urine was coming out of the tube. I’ve been drinking normally, but nothing. Then the pain started—left side, really bad, worse when I breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned nausea and vomiting—was the vomit dark or bloody?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, brownish, with little red streaks. I was really worried. I tried to adjust the tube myself, got a little urine out, but the pain got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve reviewed your history—you’ve had this tube for a while due to a stricture from your ileal conduit. It looks like it became dislodged, which caused a backup and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it just fell out? I thought it was supposed to stay in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It didn’t fully fall out, but it shifted enough to stop draining. We’ve already consulted urology. They’re going to replace it today with imaging guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that fix the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help a lot. The pain is likely from the blockage. Once urine starts draining again, the pressure will go down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had the procedure a little while ago. The urologist successfully replaced your nephrostomy tube. The imaging showed the tract was still open, and they confirmed the new tube is in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it draining now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it is. They drained clear urine from the kidney. You might see some blood-tinged drainage for a day or so—that’s normal after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I still feel some pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing your pain with your regular oxycodone and add acetaminophen. It may take a day or two for the discomfort to settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test showed signs of infection—positive nitrites and white blood cells—so we’re starting you on IV meropenem just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I don’t have a fever. Is it really an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. That’s why we’re only doing a short course. We’ll check with infectious disease and likely stop it if you stay afebrile and your labs don’t show infection signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I was on meropenem, I got a rash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that in your record. We’ll watch closely. If any rash appears, we’ll stop it and switch to something else. Your safety comes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back—no growth from the catheterized sample. The earlier one showed mixed flora, but that’s likely contamination.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It doesn’t look like it. You’re not running a fever, and your white count is normal. We’re going to stop the meropenem today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But I still hurt. Is it just from the blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. The kidney was swollen from the backup. Now that it’s draining, it should improve. We’ll keep your pain meds going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs look good. Creatinine was up a bit—3.5 from your baseline of around 3.1—but it’s likely from dehydration and the obstruction. It’s already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my kidney okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no permanent damage. This was acute-on-chronic, but it’s resolving with treatment. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been discussing your case with your urologist, Dr. ___. He recommends you follow up in clinic to talk about surgical options for the stricture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Surgery? I thought the tube was the solution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube helps, but you’ve had two hospitalizations now due to complications. Surgery might fix the stricture permanently and avoid future issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. I just want to stop having these emergencies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain is better, right? You’re moving more comfortably?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, much better. Still some ache, but not like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your kidney function is back to baseline. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not sure I’m ready. What if the tube dislodges again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. But you’re stable now. The tube is secure, and we’ll make sure you have follow-up with urology and nephrology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still on track for discharge tomorrow. Your labs are stable, pain is controlled, and you’re eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking about the surgery. What would it involve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It would be a procedure to reconstruct the connection between your ureter and the conduit. It’s not minor, but it could prevent future blockages and eliminate the need for the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to talk to the urologist about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ve already set up the appointment. He’ll go over the risks and benefits with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your discharge is approved for tomorrow morning. We’ll go over your medications and instructions today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m nervous about going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. But you’re in much better shape now. The tube is working, your pain is under control, and your kidney is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the fosfomycin? I’m still taking that weekly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that. It helps prevent infections, especially with your history. We’re keeping all your other meds the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my seizures? I’m still on Keppra.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we recommend you see neurology. You haven’t had follow-up in a while, and it’s important to keep monitoring that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. You’re doing well—clear mind, stable vitals, pain controlled. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess so. Just want to make sure I don’t end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve set up all your follow-ups—urology, nephrology, neurology. If you notice any fever, pain, or the tube stops draining, come in right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I have questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctors. Your care team has your records. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—you’re clear on your meds? Fosfomycin once a week, oxycodone every 8 hours, omeprazole twice a day, and the rest as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve got it written down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your mother is your health care proxy, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve listed her contact info in your discharge papers. She can help if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll call her when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urostomy bag had a lot of sediment. Make sure to flush it regularly and stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do, but it still builds up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with ileal conduits. The urologist can advise on ways to minimize it, maybe with dietary changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll ask him.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I understand you've been having some pain and fevers. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this left flank pain for about a week now. It’s been going down into my scrotum. And I’ve had fevers up to 102. It started after someone cut me with a razor during an assault three days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry that happened. We’ll make sure you’re safe. The pain and fever could be related to your kidney or PCN tube. We’ve already given you some pain medicine and started antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The PCN tube? It’s been draining only about 100cc yesterday. That seems low, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s low. We’re concerned the tube might not be draining well. We did a CT scan to check its position and your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my testicle? It’s swollen and tender. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your scrotum. It shows hydroceles—fluid around the testicles—but no torsion or mass. So it’s likely related to inflammation from the infection, not an emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. But I’ve been through this before. Last time it was the tube dislodged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The CT shows your left PCN tube is in the kidney, but we’re not sure if it’s optimally placed. We’ll watch your labs and drainage closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine test showed a lot of white blood cells and bacteria. We’re treating you for a kidney infection—pyelonephritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on antibiotics already, right? Which one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, IV meropenem. It’s strong and covers the likely bacteria, especially given your many allergies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time they stopped antibiotics when the tube was fixed. Will that happen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. If the infection is from poor drainage, fixing the tube might be the main fix. But we’ll wait for culture results first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure’s been high. I noticed it on the monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been running in the 160s, sometimes higher. We’ll start a blood pressure pill—amlodipine—once we’re sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back. It grew Klebsiella and E. coli. Both are sensitive to meropenem, so we’ll continue that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are those dangerous bacteria?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can be, especially with your medical history. But since they’re responding to the antibiotic, we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My pain’s a bit better, but the tube still doesn’t seem to be draining well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We agree. Your creatinine went up a little, and output is low. We’re arranging for interventional radiology to check and possibly replace the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? That’s frustrating. Is it because of the stricture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the stricture in your ureter makes drainage difficult. The PCN tube bypasses it, but it can get blocked or pulled back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiology team reviewed your case. They’ll do a nephrostogram to see where the tube is and likely exchange it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation and local numbing. Most patients feel pressure but not sharp pain. It’s usually well tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about these swollen lymph nodes? I feel them in my groin and neck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. The CT didn’t show enlarged nodes inside, and your chest X-ray is clear. We checked for infections like syphilis and STIs—those were negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible, but your LDH and uric acid are normal, which is reassuring. We’ll watch them. If they don’t go down, we might consider a biopsy later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. The procedure went well. They exchanged your left PCN tube. The old one had pulled back into a lower part of the kidney, so it wasn’t draining properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that was the problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The new tube is in the right spot. We already see better drainage—over 300cc in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. My pain’s already less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep you on antibiotics for now. Your kidney function should improve as drainage gets better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your creatinine is coming down—from 3.3 to 2.9. That’s a good sign your kidneys are recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No fever today, and your white count is stable. We’ll keep the IV antibiotics for a few more days, then switch to oral if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still on the weekly fosfomycin, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue that after discharge to help prevent future infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking better. Blood pressure is under control with amlodipine. We’ll send that home with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your urologist to discuss long-term options for the stricture. Also, primary care and orthopedics for your hip and spine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lymph nodes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor. If they persist, your doctor might order more tests. But for now, no red flags.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching your antibiotic to oral fosfomycin tomorrow. You’ll finish the course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one dose a week. It’s well tolerated and covers the bacteria we saw.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Creatinine is 2.7, and you’re off IV meds. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What supplies do I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending extra drainage bags and a device to secure the tube—StatLock—to prevent it from pulling out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on your regular oxycodone. But because of your high dose, we’re also giving you a naloxone nasal spray in case of overdose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s smart. I’ll show my mom how to use it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge today. You look great—no fever, pain controlled, eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. Just to recap—I have amlodipine for blood pressure, keep the weekly fosfomycin, and follow up with urology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And watch the lymph nodes. If they grow or new ones appear, let your doctor know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PCN tube care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Empty the bag regularly, keep the site clean and dry, and use the StatLock. Call if drainage drops or you get fever again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. You handled this well. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge paperwork. Any new pain or concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, all good. Drainage is steady, and I haven’t had a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll finalize your discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are ready. You’ll leave with prescriptions, supplies, and follow-up appointments scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in last night with fevers, chills, and your PCN tube fell out at home?

conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had flank pain and fevers too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking fluids. My pain is better since the tube was replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Proper drainage helps a lot. We’ll keep the IV antibiotics going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected in the bone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I didn’t want to be on more meds. I’ll keep cleaning it myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue to offer professional wound care, but we respect your choice. Just watch for increased redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest urine culture from the PCN tube shows no growth. That’s a great sign—the antibiotic is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No bacteria at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: You mentioned some blood in your stool the other night. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my doctor about the hemorrhoids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is back to normal, and you’re afebrile. You’re doing really well. We’re on day 8 of antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll still take the weekly fosfomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One thing—we need to talk about your PCN tube. You shouldn’t try to replace it yourself if it falls out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why not? I’ve done it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, you’re going home with naloxone. It’s a safety measure because of your high-dose oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I had that last time. I’ll keep it with me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final urine culture is negative. No growth. That means the infection is cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll give you one more dose of meropenem today, and if all goes well, discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.text: Okay. Just… make sure they know I need that follow-up.
