conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Urology will call you. And call us if you develop fever, pain, or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re here for you. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming you’re leaving with your prescriptions and follow-up details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have the fosfomycin. I’ll call urology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in clinic if needed. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good luck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your meds as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. That means a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of the hospitalists. You're in the hospital because you came in with somnolence and your nephrostomy tube had fallen out and was reinserted by you at home. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I’ve been tired, more than usual. I get like this when I’m getting sick. My tube’s been falling out a lot lately. I just pushed it back in and taped it with duct tape.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That’s not safe, because it can introduce infection. We’ve checked your labs, and your white blood cell count is elevated, which means your body is fighting an infection. Your kidney function is also worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. So that’s why I feel so off? I’ve also had a cough with brown mucus and some diarrhea the past few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those could be part of the infection. We did a CT scan, and your tube is now in the right place. But we’re concerned about a kidney infection because the tube was out and reinserted without sterile technique.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on IV antibiotics—meropenem—twice a day for 10 days. You’ll also get fluids and we’ll monitor your kidney function. Your tube was replaced earlier today by radiology to make sure it’s secure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They already changed the tube? I remember being in a room with two doctors…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was exchanged using imaging guidance. They used a StatLock to secure it this time, so it’s less likely to fall out. That’s important to prevent future infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I don’t want to be here too long. I’ve got things to do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but finishing the full course of antibiotics is crucial. If we stop early, the infection could come back stronger or become resistant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked a urine sample. It showed many bacteria, but the culture came back as contaminated—likely from skin flora. That means we can’t rely on it to guide antibiotics, so we’re treating based on your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not useful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for identifying the exact bacteria, but your symptoms and high white count confirm infection. Blood cultures were negative, which is good—no bacteria in the bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my cough? Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray. No pneumonia. Your cough might be from postnasal drip or irritation. We’ll keep an eye on it. The brown sputum could be old blood from coughing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it. Given your history of C. diff, we’ll test if it worsens. For now, we’ll keep you hydrated and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white count is already coming down—from 12.7 to 6.1. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s encouraging, but you’ve only had one day of antibiotics. We recommend completing all 10 days. We discussed placing a midline so you could finish IV antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wait, you’re kicking me out? I thought I was supposed to stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. We want you to stay or go home with IV antibiotics. The midline would let you receive meropenem at home safely. But it’s your choice.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want that. I just want to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but leaving now increases the risk of the infection returning, getting worse, or spreading. It could lead to sepsis or even be life-threatening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hear you, but I’m feeling better. I’ve dealt with this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still, we strongly advise against leaving. If you do, you’ll need to follow up urgently with urology and infectious disease. Your kidney function was impaired—creatinine 4.4—but it’s improving now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs continue to improve. CRP, a marker of inflammation, dropped from 111 to 64. Your creatinine is now 3.9. Your body is responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So can I leave today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re improving, but you’re only on day three of a 10-day course. Stopping now risks incomplete treatment. We still recommend finishing the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: CRP is now 35, and your white count is normal. Your infection is resolving. But again, we’re only on day four. Please consider staying or using the midline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve made up my mind. I’m leaving. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I have to inform you this would be against medical advice. You understand the risks—worsening infection, resistance, hospitalization, or death?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I understand. But I’m leaving anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll prepare discharge instructions. You must follow up with urology to discuss surgical options—this keeps happening because of your anatomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, they’ve been saying that. But I don’t want surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s the best way to prevent repeated infections. Also, keep the StatLock on the tube and never reinsert it yourself. Call us if it comes out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your regular doses—OxyContin 60 mg every 8 hours and oxycodone as needed. Also, acetaminophen for fever or mild pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my seizure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Levetiracetam twice daily—don’t miss doses. Same for your anxiety—clonazepam as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my stomach medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Omeprazole daily. And sevelamer with meals for your phosphate levels. Sodium bicarbonate twice daily for your acid levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mom knows?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve contacted her. She’s aware you’re leaving AMA and will support you at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, you left the hospital yesterday morning before we could finalize your discharge. We tried to reach you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I left a note. I’m home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please confirm you’ll follow up with urology and infectious disease. Your care team is concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call them. I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. Have you made your appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. I’m feeling okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please don’t delay. Your infection isn’t fully treated. Call today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, this is your final follow-up call. You were admitted on October 12th for a kidney infection due to your nephrostomy tube falling out and being reinserted non-sterilely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I remember.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your treatment was going well—labs improved—but you left against medical advice on the fourth day, before finishing IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. But please follow up as discussed. Your health depends on it. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You were brought in because your nephrostomy tube came out and you're having pain. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had pain at the site for about a month. Today, the tube started leaking, then it just fell out. I felt a jolt when my wheelchair cushion popped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’re having pain from your left flank down to your lower abdomen, right? Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, throbbing pain, worse when I cough. I’ve been feeling hot and cold, and I threw up earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We did a CT scan, and it shows your left kidney is swollen because the tube wasn’t draining well. That’s likely why you’re in pain and feeling sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the tube wasn’t working even before it fell out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The tip was in the right place, but it wasn’t draining properly. That can cause infection and kidney stress. We’ve scheduled a procedure to replace it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it be more secure this time? It keeps coming loose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the interventional radiologist will use extra sutures and a StatLock device to hold it in place better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I don’t want this happening every few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The tube was successfully replaced. It’s draining well now, and the imaging confirms it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Is the infection from the kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your urine showed lots of bacteria and white blood cells. We’re calling it pyelonephritis—kidney infection. We’ve started IV antibiotics, meropenem, twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is it the same one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same antibiotic as last time. Your urine culture came back contaminated, so we’re going with what’s worked before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Contaminated? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the sample had skin or genital bacteria, so we can’t trust which bug is really causing the infection. But given your symptoms, we’re treating it seriously.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. How long will I be on IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Five days total. You’ll get it through your IV twice a day. We’ll monitor your labs to see how you’re responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white blood cell count is coming down, which means the infection is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My pain is better too, especially since the new tube is in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We also looked at your leg swelling. You mentioned a fall two months ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I fell getting into my car. My leg’s been swollen since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows a healing fracture in your left tibia. It’s not new, but it’s still recovering. No need for a brace, but we recommend elevation and compression socks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not broken now? Just healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. It’s a subacute fracture—meaning it’s in the healing phase. Ortho says no surgery needed. We also checked for blood clots—your ultrasound was negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. The swelling’s been worrying me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is stable. Creatinine is still around 4.0, which is typical for you. We’re watching it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the tube issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. The blockage made it worse—acute on chronic kidney injury. But now that the tube is working, your kidneys should handle things better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure’s still high. I see it’s up there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping you on amlodipine. Your pressures are spiking to the 180s, so your outpatient doctor might need to adjust your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all goes well. You’ve had four doses of IV antibiotics. There’s one more due.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not keep the IV. Can I take pills instead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can switch to oral fosfomycin. It’s the same family—just three doses, every other day. But it’s important you finish all of them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take the script. I don’t want another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you the prescription. We offered to call the pharmacy to check coverage, but you can do it yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll handle it. Just give me the script.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs look good. White count is normal. You’re down to just mild tenderness at the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leg swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Better with elevation and compression. Vascular surgery said no concern for compartment syndrome. Keep wearing the socks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my hip wound? It’s not getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wound care checked it. It’s a chronic ulcer, not infected now. They recommend continuing home care. Surgery isn’t an option right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll keep cleaning it like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. We’ll review your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, take the fosfomycin—three doses, every other day. It’s critical to finish all of them to prevent the infection from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. I’ll do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Second, call interventional radiology to schedule your next tube check in a few months. We gave you extra drainage bags and a StatLock to help prevent dislodgement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call them today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, keep elevating your left leg and wearing the compression socks. Follow up with ortho in a month for another X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your home medications—pain, seizure, anxiety, and kidney meds. Your blood pressure is still high, so talk to your doctor about adjusting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. If you develop fever, increased pain, or the tube comes out again, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to be back here soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your care team and your mother is listed as your health care proxy. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep the number handy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, the discharge papers are ready. A nurse will go over them with you one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I feel a lot better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine tested positive for cocaine. You mentioned you didn’t use it. Is that correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I haven’t used in months. Maybe it’s from old residue or something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll note that. Just wanted to check in case you needed support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate it. I’m clean now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're in the hospital because of left flank pain, fevers, and your nephrostomy tube isn’t draining well. We did a quick ultrasound in the ER and saw that your left kidney is very swollen. We’re concerned this is due to a blockage in your PCN tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s been hurting more than usual. The tube’s been draining less, and I’ve felt feverish. Is that why my kidney’s swollen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The tube is supposed to drain urine from your kidney, but it looks blocked. That’s causing pressure and infection. We’ve scheduled a procedure to replace it tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had this before. But this time it feels worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your white blood cell count is elevated, and your urine from the tube was cloudy. That suggests a significant infection. We’ll start IV antibiotics once the tube is replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on a lot of meds already. Will they interact?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your list. You’re on meropenem, which is safe given your allergies. We’ll adjust doses for your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had the PCN tube exchange this morning. It went well. The old tube was clogged and partially pulled out. We placed a new one, and 250 cc of cloudy fluid drained out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot. Was it infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we sent it for culture. In the meantime, you’re on IV meropenem to treat the infection. Your pain should start improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still hurting pretty bad. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve ordered IV Dilaudid for breakthrough pain. We’ll monitor your intake since you’re not eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your kidney function is stable—creatinine is 4.1, which is your baseline. We’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want it getting worse. What about the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re waiting on culture results. For now, meropenem is covering the likely bacteria. We’ll adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound yesterday. No abscess, and the left kidney isn’t hydronephrotic anymore. That means the new tube is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My pain is a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw your kidneys are echogenic, which fits with your chronic kidney disease. Nothing new there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture from your PCN fluid came back. It grew Staphylococcus aureus, but it’s methicillin-sensitive, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s treatable. We’re switching from meropenem to IV daptomycin, which works well for this bug. You’ll need a 14-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fourteen days? I’ll have to stay here that long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ideally, yes. We can arrange a PICC line so you can get antibiotics at home, or go to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want a PICC. I’ve had infections before. And I can’t go to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. But stopping early could lead to relapse. We’ll discuss options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium is high—6.1. It’s something we watch with kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can affect your heart, but your EKG is normal. We’d like to give you kayexalate to bring it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I can’t. It gives me terrible diarrhea, and I already struggle with bowel issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. We’ll monitor it and recheck tomorrow. You should check it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood cultures came back negative. That’s good—means the infection is likely localized to the kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looks like it. Your white count is coming down. But you’ve only had 5 days of daptomycin. You need 14.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, but I can’t stay. I’ll take it at home somehow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spoken with urology. Your PCN is draining well. They’ll see you as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my leg? It’s been aching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ortho reviewed your old fracture. You have a healing tibia fracture. They recommend follow-up, but no urgent action.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t gone yet. I’ll try to make the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on day 7 of antibiotics. Your creatinine is stable at 3.9, and potassium is 6.0—still high but not worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better, but still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Infection takes a toll. We’re planning to taper your IV pain meds and switch back to your oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need those for pain. Don’t stop them too fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. But we need to prepare for discharge. We’re concerned about finishing the antibiotic course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll manage it. I don’t want to stay longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is day 8 of antibiotics. We’ve discussed options: home health, outpatient infusion, or stopping early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want any of those. I’ll take my chances.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We strongly advise completing the course. Incomplete treatment could lead to relapse or resistance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but I’m leaving. I’ve been here too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll document your decision. Please follow up with urology, nephrology, and check your potassium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. I know I need to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been informed you’re planning to leave. We want to make sure you know the risks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve made up my mind. I’m not staying for two more weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your PCN is working, pain is better, and labs are stable. But you’ve only had 8 of 14 antibiotic days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll rest at home. I’ll call if I get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. And follow up with your doctors. Your urine test also showed cocaine. We’re concerned about your use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I lost a close friend. I’ve been struggling. I slipped back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sorry to hear that. We’ve connected you with counseling resources. Please consider reaching out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I know I need help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself. We’ll send your records to your providers. Please come back if you develop fever, pain, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, you were supposed to be discharged this morning, but we’ve been informed you left the hospital last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had to go. I couldn’t stay any longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand, but it’s important you follow up. Your infection isn’t fully treated, and your potassium is still high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I’ll call urology. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. And consider speaking with someone about your loss and substance use. You’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your discharge plan. You eloped before formal discharge, but we’re documenting your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just needed to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We respect that. Just remember: finish your follow-ups, check your potassium, and call if you’re not feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope not either. Take care of yourself, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your PCN is functioning, infection markers improved, but antibiotic course incomplete. Follow-up critical.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the calls today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your meds list and records. Please stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll be okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve finalized your discharge. You’ve completed 8 of 14 antibiotic days. Please follow up as discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. Stay safe, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve documented your elopement. Please contact us if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want this to happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope not. Take care of yourself, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in after your nephrostomy tube came out. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it fell out last night. I’ve had this pressure in my left side all day. It’s been killing me. I know when something’s wrong with my tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you. That kind of pain is serious, especially with your history. We’ve reviewed your labs and are arranging for a new tube to be placed today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just need it fixed. But I’m also feeling shaky, nauseous… I haven’t had my pain meds in two days. I take OxyContin and oxycodone at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could explain some of the symptoms—withdrawal from opioids can cause nausea, anxiety, and sweating. We’ll manage that carefully while making sure your pain is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not trying to get high. I just need what I take every day. I don’t want to feel like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re not judging you. We’ll give you a safe dose to help with withdrawal and pain. Your safety comes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my urine’s been cloudy, lots of sediment. I think I’ve got another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a urine sample. It shows white blood cells and bacteria, which suggests infection. But the culture might be contaminated, so we’re cautious about interpreting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So are you going to treat it or not? I’ve been through this before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of recurrent UTIs and the symptoms, we’re starting antibiotics just in case. We’ll adjust based on further results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my kidney numbers—they’re always high. Is it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 4.3, which is elevated, and your bicarbonate is low at 10. That means your kidneys aren’t clearing acid well—metabolic acidosis. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but we’re watching it. It’s partly due to your chronic kidney disease, which is stage 5 now. We’ll support your body while we fix the tube issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stage 5? That’s not good, is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means your kidney function is quite low. You’re not on dialysis yet, but nephrology will help us decide next steps. Right now, we focus on the acute issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Just fix the tube. That’s what keeps me out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiology team just placed a new nephrostomy tube. The procedure went well. They confirmed severe hydronephrosis—your kidney was very swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it in the right place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, imaging shows it’s positioned correctly and draining well. That pressure you felt should start improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. It still hurts where they put it in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We’ll keep your pain managed. We’re also giving IV fluids carefully—your kidneys can’t handle too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my magnesium? I’ve been low before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your magnesium is 1.5, which is low. We’re giving a replacement slowly through the IV to bring it up safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. The acidosis is less severe today—your bicarbonate is up to 14.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s better, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It means your body is starting to balance the acid levels. We’re continuing the same treatment—antibiotics, pain control, and monitoring the tube output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. The flank pressure is gone. Still tired, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You’ve been through a lot. Your hemoglobin is low at 9.3, which explains the fatigue. It’s due to chronic kidney disease—your body doesn’t make enough red blood cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your levels are stable. We’ll manage it with medications long-term if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the infection? Are the antibiotics working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re treating it as a urinary tract infection. The culture showed E. coli, but there was contamination, so we’re relying more on your symptoms and history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I told you I knew I had one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were right. We’re using an antibiotic that covers E. coli effectively. You’re responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another good day. Your vitals are stable, the tube is draining well, and labs continue to improve. We’re thinking about discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Discharge? I still feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re much better than when you came in. The acute issue is resolved. You’ll need support at home, and we’ll arrange nursing visits to check the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I live alone. I manage, but it’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll connect you with home health. They’ll help with the tube care and check for infections. You must keep your urology and nephrology appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I know. But sometimes I miss them. Things come up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I get that. But missing appointments puts you at risk for another emergency. We want to prevent that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. What about my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prescribe your usual doses. Take them as directed. If you need more help, we can refer you to pain management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. We’ve arranged home nursing, and your prescriptions are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I feel better. But I don’t like being discharged so fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’re stable, and staying longer won’t help. The key is following up. Call us if the tube stops draining, you get a fever, or the pain comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll try to make the appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Take care of yourself, Mr. ___. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your urine has protein in it, which is common with kidney disease. Keep monitoring it with your nephrologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that leading to dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Many people live with stage 5 CKD for years without dialysis. It depends on how your body adapts and how well we manage things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we can ask. Stay in touch, and don’t wait to call if something feels wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. The discharge papers are with the nurse. Someone will help you out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—no heavy lifting near the tube site. Keep the area clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know the drill. I’ve had this tube for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Just wanted to reinforce it. We want to avoid another dislodgement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.
